title: Hand Lamp
passages:
The lamp had gone cold in her fingers, the filament dead from the jolt when the brakes let go. Miko pinched the base — thumb and forefinger on the contact points, the way Wren taught her — and the bulb coughed yellow back to life. She hung it on the crew box's lip, then swung her legs over the side.

Her boots hit the spur's deck plates. Cold steel through the soles. Her knees locked, then unlocked, the sixty miles of vibration finally catching up. Dust coated her coat sleeves, gray as the rig's blank plates. Two coast tickets still zipped in the inner pocket, the graphite names she'd paid for: J. Renner, M. Kestrel. The third name rode in Saul's pocket somewhere back at the jaw.

Kass stood at the spur's end, pedal-rail leaned against the rail, one boot propped on the tie. The work light Saul had pinned her with cut a hard cone across her face. She looked like she'd ridden the bearing seizure all the way in — sweat dark at her collar, dust in the lines around her eyes.

"You're heavy," Kass said. "For a ghost."

Miko flexed her fingers, feeling the stiffness. "You're slow. For a dispatcher."

"Bearing seized at the nine-kilometer mark. Coasted the last two klicks."

"Should've greased it."

"Should've walked."

Miko snorted. The sound caught in her throat, too close to a laugh. She looked past Kass to the rig's forward canister. The clamp ring ticked — *tick, tick, tick* — each sound a tooth engaging on the cold-cycle lockout. No reader could open it once the cycle seated. The canister would become a sealed drum, dead weight on a dead spur.

"Sixty miles," Miko said, not looking at Kass. "I didn't ride sixty miles for the coast."

The wind off the ore line carried the smell of cold iron and something burning — Brill's stove, maybe, or the storeroom's generator. Behind them, the jaw gaped dark. The hand lamp threw long shadows across the deck plates.

Miko's hand found the zipper of her inner pocket. Two tickets. Two names that weren't hers. She'd bought them with three shifts of hazard pay and a favor owed to a coast puller who didn't ask questions.

"Then what'd you ride for?" Kass asked. Quiet. The banter dropped.

Miko didn't answer. She walked toward the ticking canister, the lamp swinging from her fingers, and the deck plates rang under her boots.

The jaw plate sat twenty meters on, a steel throat bolted to the spur's end with a reader head mounted like a gun sight. Saul stood beside it, clipboard in hand, the work light hooked to their belt throwing their shadow long across the tracks. Behind them, the storeroom door was shut — a slab of plate steel with a viewing slit at eye level and a chalked name above it: BRILL. No crescent mark cut into the plate. Just the name.

Odessa Brill stood in the slit's rectangle, forearms crossed on the sill. Her face was a mask of grease and wind-burn, eyes flat under the brim of her cap. She didn't move when Miko stopped at the plate's edge, the hand lamp casting her face in a swing of yellow.

"Station rule," Saul said, not looking up from their clipboard. "Unlogged rig, unsealed cargo, no manifest. You're a stowaway. Cargo's seized pending trust review."

Miko set the lamp on the deck plate. The ticking from the forward canister punched through the quiet — *tick, tick, tick* — each one a fraction of a second closer to a seal no key could break.

"Eleven seals," she said. Her voice carried flat across the spur. "Struck short out of Kettering Bay 4, Shift 2. Crescent receiving mark. Same mark Nour used at Anza's jaw to pay Culvert Nine's resupply. You want the count? Canister one, Bay 4 stamp, reader logged 04:12. Two, 04:18. Three — "

"Stowaway," Saul repeated. They tapped the clipboard. "Rule thirteen. Unauthorized personnel on rolling stock. Theft of node cargo. I'm logging you now."

"Four, 04:31. Five, 04:37. Six, 04:43 — "

"Shut it."

"Seven, 04:49. Eight, 04:55. Nine, 05:01. Ten, 05:07. Eleven, 05:13 — all struck full at Anza's jaw, all logged to Culvert Nine's reader, all paid for with Nour's chalk." Miko stepped up to the plate, close enough to read the pitting in the steel. "These cans aren't stolen cargo. They're Anza's resupply payment. Eleven warm canisters for forty mouths through winter. You seize them, your people eat cold rations until spring."

Brill didn't blink. "The throat opens on a matched seal. Crescent mark on the plate, crescent mark on the can. No match, no throat."

"There's a crescent die at Kettering," Miko said. "Chipped. V. Ospina holds it. The mark it cuts — " She reached out, fingers hovering over the door plate's blank steel. " — isn't on your door."

Brill's eyes didn't move. "Then the throat stays shut."

"Then eleven cans freeze on this deck," Miko said. "And forty names on your chalk stay crosses."

Saul wrote something on their clipboard. Torn the sheet off. Held it out toward the viewing slit. "Stowaway logged. Cargo seized. Trust review pending Kettering desk."

The wind shifted. From the storeroom behind Brill came a sound — thin through the steel, a voice — but Brill didn't look back.

Miko didn't argue. She turned to the switch stand at the spur's heel — a lever frozen in the diverge position, its handle rusted to the curve that had sent the rig onto the dead track. Kass was already moving, dropping the work light from their belt and hooking it to the switch's base so the beam caught the pivot point.

"Come-along's in the rig's tool box," Miko said. "If the brakes held on the grade."

"Brakes dumped," Kass said. "That's how we got here."

"Then we're the brakes."

They climbed the rig's side ladder together, Miko's boots finding the rungs by memory, Kass's fingers white on the rail. The crew box smelled of cold oil and the hand lamp's dying filament. The tool box sat bolted to the bulkhead — Miko wrenched it open, the latch screaming in the quiet, and pulled the come-along free. Steel cable, ratchet handle, two hooks black with grease. Heavy in her hands.

"Anchor it to the jaw's foot," she said, tossing one end to Kass. "I'll hook the rig's tow eye."

Kass caught it, stumbled on the deck plate, recovered. The cable paid out behind them as they walked the length of the rig — eleven canisters, each one a cylinder of insulated steel two meters long, welded to the frame in a line that stretched the spur's full forty meters. The forward canister's ticking had slowed. *Tick. Tick. Tick.* The interval stretching. The lockout cycling deeper.

Miko hooked the come-along to the tow eye at the rig's aft end. The metal was warm under her fingers — residual heat from the canisters, bleeding into the frame. She ratcheted the slack out, the mechanism clicking loud in the wind.

"Ready?" she called.

Kass stood at the jaw's foot, the cable taut between gloved hands, boots braced against the rail. The switch lever waited behind them, the points still set for the spur. "Throw it," Kass said. "I'll hold tension."

Miko ran back to the switch. The lever fought her — rust and cold and the weight of the points themselves. She threw her shoulder into it, feet sliding on the ballast, and the mechanism groaned, then snapped over with a sound like a bone breaking. The points clicked home. The rig sat aligned with the jaw now, a straight shot twenty meters to the reader head.

"Walk it," Miko said.

They pulled. The come-along's ratchet screamed. The rig moved — inches at first, the dead bearing on the forward truck grinding metal on metal, a shriek that cut through the wind. Then a lurch, and the mass committed. Ten tons of steel and pressurized nitrogen rolling on one live truck and one dead one.

Kass's boots dug trenches in the ballast. The cable sang under tension. Miko added her weight at the rig's side, pushing against the cold frame, her boots finding purchase on the ties. The rig gained speed — slow, inexorable, the dead bearing howling now, a sound that lived in the teeth.

"Easy," Kass gasped. "Easy — "

The rig didn't know easy. It knew momentum. The dead bearing seized harder, the friction spiking, and the rig jerked — a violent shudder that ran the length of the frame. Kass's feet flew out. The cable snapped taut. Miko saw the dispatcher go down hard, one leg caught between rail and tie, the come-along handle whipping free and spinning — 

Miko let go of the rig. Dropped to her knees beside Kass. "Leg — "

"Pull," Kass gritted out. "The reader. Flood it. *Now.*"

Miko looked. The jaw's reader head loomed ten meters ahead — a glass eye mounted on a steel stalk, dark and waiting. The rig would hit it in seconds. She scrambled up, ran the last stretch, the hand lamp clutched in both hands. The rig's crew box passed her, the forward canister's clamp ring visible through the window — the lockout teeth engaged now, a silver spiral biting into the seal ring.

She reached the reader stalk. The glass face was cold, dead. She pressed the hand lamp flat against it, the yellow beam flooding straight into the sensor.

The glass woke.

Amber light bloomed behind the face, spreading like a bruise. The reader's internal mechanism whirred — a sound Miko had heard a thousand times at Anza's jaw, the hunt beginning. The beam swept the rig's plates as they rolled past: blank steel, blank steel, blank steel. No crescent. No stamp. No mark at all.

The amber flickered. Hunted. Found nothing.

The light dropped to dark.

A chime sounded from the reader stalk — three notes, descending. The throat's log display, a strip of e-ink bolted to the steel, refreshed: *CARGO LOGGED — UNSEALED — NO MANIFEST — PENDING REVIEW.*

The rig rolled past, into the throat's dark mouth. The clamp ring on the forward canister took its final bite. The lockout seated with a sound like a door slamming shut.

Miko stood breathing hard, the hand lamp trembling in her grip. Behind her, Kass was hauling themself upright, favoring the left leg, the come-along cable slack and useless on the ballast.

"Logged as cargo," Kass said. Voice flat. "Not resupply. Cargo."

Miko looked at the storeroom door. The viewing slit was dark. Brill wasn't watching.

"Then we make it resupply," Miko said. "Or we watch eleven cans rot."

The second canister's clamp ring began to tick.
